utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there are, I think, three areas, as I recollect, to be discussed; three village dossiers, the tape evidence, and I think, in general, transcripts. I don't know what order is most convenient. The shorter, possibly, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I make a proposal? Apart from matters of information that I must provide, can I suggest we turn then to the tapes and from the tape to the transcripts, because the transcript issue feeds into or will have consequences for the binder issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can take, as it were, them together, but it clearly would be sensible to deal with the tape first as it is the matter which is freshest in our mind and we have to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I, before I come to the tape, deal with a couple of outstanding issues. Affidavit so-called evidence, the Chamber will remember that I mentioned at the beginning of the week that we have finally been informed of the possibility of a request going to Bosnia for the appointment of a Judge who will authenticate signatures. I said at the beginning of the week we will make the request ourselves unless, if the Chamber givers thought to it, the Chamber would prefer to issue the instruction itself, and in any event, the request will have to go or possibly be followed by statements of witnesses and, of course, provision of statements of witnesses to a third party is something that really needs the court sanction. The position is that we have a request that we are in a position to forward today with some witness statements attached to it, and if the Chamber is not itself disposed to seek the appointment itself of a Judge, if it's had a chance to think about it, then we will forward that request, but we would seek leave of the Chamber to append witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly it must be done as quickly as possible. It would seem more expeditious if the Prosecution undertook the task rather than doing it via the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we'll do. You can have leave, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of the four witnesses who had not responded to subpoenas, there was one in respect of whom I notified your Legal Officer I would give further consideration in light of the pressures of time. We consider, in light of those pressures, that it's not justified to seek an affidavit against that one. I can name him. It's the name Ribo. So we don't seek any further action in respect of Ribo. The next point relates to the map provider, Elford. The Defence for Mr. Kordic have served a Rule 94 cross-notice. I suppose seeking, thereby, to both establish that he's an expert and then to try and prove that he's not an expert; a highly technical point. We don't advance him as an expert. He may, in fact, have expertise. I don't know. Lots of people, when they come to the witness box to give evidence of fact suddenly give bits of evidence of expertise and technical points that aren't taken. So the mere serving of a counter-notice isn't going to achieve some fascinating technical success for the Defence that they might have hoped. They ask for his background. I said I'll provide it without prejudice. I gather he's got degrees in international relations and was an analyst in the Army for a time. He's here as an Army Analyst. No doubt if the negotiation seems to be attractive to Mr. Kovacic, not attractive to those representing Mr. Kordic, they'll be in a position, if it's necessary, for him to be called and him to be cross-examined. That's really as far as I can go on that. As far as tapes are concerned, we've had the tape listened to by a language speaker. We understand them to be identical. Mr. Stein tells me otherwise and that there are two bleeps or electronic bleeps on one tape and not on the other. Our language assistant tells us they are present on both. I recollect hearing, I think on one tape, if I've got it right, a sound that happens sometimes when a mobile phone is near to an electronic device, but that's all I can recollect. Mr. Stein tells us that the conversations 10 and 11 are missing. Again, that doesn't accord with our understanding. We understand that they are entirely parallel, one with the other. But I understand that Mr. Stein accepts that apart from those two matters, of which he may make observation, the tapes are, indeed, identical. Our language assistant tells us that there may be some difficulty with or divergence of the index, and probably at the point I had difficulty with the conversations, but that's as far as any comment he has to make is made available to you. So I would ask us to get on with the argument about the tape and bring it to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. May it please the Court, first with regard to Mr. Elford, the map expert. It is my hope that by next Monday we will have worked all matters out. However, in an exercise of caution, Mr. Elford is a military analyst. His report, at first reading, is not merely about maps. It's about troop strengths and troop movements, and it's clearly an analysis of testimony in other Tribunal cases, including the testimony of General Blaskic. Except to note my exception to what Mr. Nice just said, I don't want to burden the Court further on something that may be moot. With regard to the audiotape, I'd like to state my own position, as opposed to having the Prosecutor state it for me. This issue gets curiouser and curiouser. The tape that I have before me, the one that was given to us by the Prosecution which has now been marked into evidence as Exhibit Number 2801.1, that which the Prosecutor supplied to us is distinctly less audible than the copy which was given to us by the witness and made a copy of, so I would like Your Honour to consider the following: First, the copy's quality is at wide variance. Second, there are two electronic noises -- I don't know what they are -- on the copy that we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts in the tapes do the electronic noises appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As to the first electronic noise, if you turn to Document 2801.2A, Z2801.2A, which is the Croatian transcript, it's on page 2, line 13. And using that same document, there's also an electronic noise at the end of the first side, which would be side B, which would be on page 18. I don't know what they mean, but I'm not prepared to say what they are or are not. Moreover, if we can turn to the English version, 2801.2B, and compare the English version with Exhibit 2801.3, which is the index of the tapes, according to the witness, if Your Honour recalls, the index was prepared contemporaneously to the recording. The index purports to show that there were nine tapes transposed from microcassettes on -- I'm sorry, 11 tapes transposed, 11 recordings transposed from microcassettes on side A, and they are listed 1 through 11 on Exhibit 2801.3. And then on side B, there are three tapes that have been transposed from the microcassette to the larger cassette. That index is referenced at the witness's ICTY statement dated 4 December 1999 at the last page, and that is a listing of the same evidence that appears at 2801.3. When listening to the English -- I'm sorry, when listening to the tape and following it in either English or Croatian, you get to, on the Croatian version, page 17 -- that would be 2801.2 -- and on the English, page 18, and that's the end of the ninth conversation, that conversation allegedly being between Mr. Pero and Mr. D. Grubesic. Numbers 10 and 11 don't exist. You'll find on the English transcript, at page 18 and page 19, that which is on the tape, and that which is on the tape is not only inaudible but it's clearly not two conversations. There's no break. It's very short, no more than 30 or 40 seconds, and it certainly does not consistently follow that which is on the index as listed on Exhibit 2801.3, nor on the witness's statement. Indeed, Mr. Nice, when he was ticking off for you exactly where each statement occurred, mentioned at Day 118, the LiveNote version at line 98 -- and I believe the full transcript version would be at page 13754 -- that he didn't know himself where conversations 10 and 11 were. Indeed, he said, "Conversation 9 starts on page 14, line 9, goes on to page 18, line 25," so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stein, could you clarify for the Trial Chamber, because either you are challenging -- well, you've been asked to verify things yourself to see whether the tapes are all right, as such, and there isn't too much of a difficulty in respect of the tapes and the relationship with the transcript. If you are challenging them, you've got to state that, and at that point we can -- as we have provided for, we will ask for a professional translator to write a report about it as quickly as possible. We're not going to go into each line and page by page and types of conversation at this hearing. There's no reason; it's pointless. My question is also to know whether if you are challenging this, you've got to say it. Now, are you also challenging the fact -- that's what we're interested in is not the other conversations but rather the conversation where the accused are involved, or the accused Mr. Kordic specifically, and I would conclude by saying are you challenging that this is also the accused on the recording that you listened to? Is that the accused on the recording in question? Are you challenging that as well or do you accept that? If there is a detailed problem that you are challenging in respect of the type of transcription, then you've got to give it to a professional. We're not going to do it here in the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me respond to both. As to taking the tapes to a professional, the only part of the tapes that should be taken to the professional is page 18 through 19 of the English. There simply is no tape conversation as set forth in the Prosecutor's proffer at 10 or 11, as to whether or not Mr. Kordic appears, his voice appears at some but not all of the recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the relevant part is the first conversation. Is there any dispute about any part of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There is a dispute in the sense of this, Your Honour: We don't dispute that Mr. Kordic's voice appears on that tape. Whether or not it was sliced and diced, put in, we do not accept. And the reason we don't accept it is just the surrounding issues of this tape itself. If you recall the testimony, this was one recording that went on on 24 January, 1993, allegedly the most interesting recording. There were others that went on before. There were times the tape machine was turned on and turned off. The witness who proffered the tape never heard the original conversation, and these conversations were all recorded by individuals under his command. If they have the electronics to listen in, they certainly have the electronics to put together the snatches of conversations. We don't know the time and, indeed, it is in many instances inaudible. Whether it's inaudible because you can't hear or they turned the tape on and turned off is unclear. Additionally, the recording then starts off on February 22nd. A full month of electronic surveillance, and then all of a sudden, on the 22nd of February through to the 25th, they're recording for three days running. Now, this goes directly to integrity, and I'd ask Your Honours to consider this: The witness testified that he was under instructions to give up the tape recording in 1993 -- 1996. Pardon me. He testified and his statement is that he gave up the recording to his superiors in the Intelligence Unit. He says, however, he kept something, a copy, and it's unclear whether he kept a copy or the original recording. That's a disparity all over the record. It defies belief and common sense that he would keep the first recording, the original recording, and turn over a copy to archives and his superior. Moreover, it further defies belief that in 1999, this being the only souvenir of the war that he kept, he would again use the came process and turn over to his superiors a third copy, having kept the second. So that what we have in court should be a copy of a copy, and the sound should get progressively worse, but that which we copied today, that which was given to us by the witness, is clearer than that which was given to the ICTY. So it's in confusion. My last point, of course, is the A/B point. And as Mr. Nice again acknowledged, the witness indicates he's recording on side A, but as the transcript shows you, side B is that which is coming to us. Now, is that just a transcription error, a plopping in the tape error? I don't know but I don't think so. If you're taping with new tape equipment, you start with side A. That which appears on the transcript is side B. So the integrity of the process is still being called into question. There are large gaps in the chain of custody of this, allowing for electronic tampering. The witness himself is incredible. In terms of all the souvenirs that he kept this is the only one, and he used it for training purposes, according to his testimony. He kept it for training purposes, but he never trained anyone with it. Then miraculously, in 1999, when they need evidence, he turns it over to his superior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, you refer to the possibility of your client's voice being sliced, diced, and put in. Is there any technology that can determine that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I believe if you have the original tape you can determine the technology. I don't purport to be an expert, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anything else, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, sir. I encourage the Court, if the Court is going to have a translator listen to this, only to listen to those two relevant segments to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is the translator going to help us? Because it's not a translation question. You say there is a sound on the tape, and you say the two parts are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's right. And you won't find Mr. Kordic's or Blaskic's voices in 10 or 11 -- in 10, Kordic and Petkovic in 11. It's noted that those are conversations between the two of them, but you won't be able to find that or hear that. So that which -- if anybody is going to check anything, it should be limited to that on page, although I don't think that takes us very far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pages 18 and the top of 19, in our transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly. Line -- well, you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They don't seem to be -- I mean, I note it's described as the conversation starts: "Put the Colonel on. Hello, Dario." but I don't suppose it's going to take anybody very much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is, in fact, I think I'm right in saying, having looked at this transcript, there is one conversation which is of importance, possibly another of marginal importance it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the point I forgot. Thank you for jogging my memory. The most important conversation, I think, the Prosecution wants to focus on, and the Court, is the first, which is clear. All of it's perfectly audible save one part, but the rest aren't, and I ask Your Honours to consider that as well. Same device, same technology, same process. It should be the same relative result. It's curiouser and curiouser. Same line, same telephone, same micro-cassette, same major cassette. Now, we're always handicapped six years later recreating what happened, and of course we're absolutely handicapped without the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm looking at the clock. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure this is, as it were, the concluded argument on admissibility or if we're at an interim --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to consider it, but if you want to add something, do. We'll consider -- there are two things, really, and there are two possible ways of going forward. One is to decide the matter now. The other one is to call for further investigation. But as I've indicated to Mr. Stein, I'm not sure there is any useful investigation which we could undertake. It's not a translation question, it's a question about a bleep and something missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As between the tapes, the only further easy exercise that could be engaged in here is for representatives of each side, who apparently held different views and each speak the language, to sit down and listen to the tapes and come to an agreement as to there is or there isn't a passage there. That shouldn't be, in itself, difficult, and that shouldn't hold up proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- technical nature -- first apology of the day to the interpreters. I suggest that they have a red card in each window that they put up or rap on the window and I would be happy to oblige. Very sorry. As to other inquiries, frankly inappropriate at this stage of the trial, and a reflection of just how completely inappropriate this application to exclude is, Mr. Stein says things about electronic facilities and electronic tampering. He's had the tape for some time, and we know they have the resources. Either it is or is it is not capable of being established whether there has been electronic tampering. It may well be that it is possible. Your Honours have heard this tape, in part, the critical conversation, it may be possible to say whether there's an electronic tampering. Of course, what would happen and what should happen is that the tape should be admitted. We have provided every material that we can, and the matter can then be taken forward. Had there been full and complete challenges, as there should have been, to the witness, then we would have been in a position ourselves to consider do we call further evidence? For example, we can call the people who took the original micro-cassettes. At the moment, on the evidence, effectively unchallenged, of the witness, we don't have to. But if they're really going to challenge, cut it, slicing and dicing, we can call the makers of the cassettes. If there's going to be a frank as opposed to a smeared allegation of slicing and dicing, we can consider whether at this stage it's worth calling a scientist. Alternatively, the tape goes in and we await further evidence, if Mr. Kordic gives evidence and says that he never said these things. Why then the matter arises for rebuttal. But one way or another, the evidence has to go in. And can I make this point: It simply won't do, in our respectful submission, to deal with the witness in the way he was dealt with. I have no doubt he's willing to come back after such treatment by innuendo and not dealt with frankly. Mr. Kordic must know not whether he said these particular words, for, of course, nobody would suggest that you'd have that memory, but he must know absolutely whether at the time concerned he was being addressed in the way spoken of as a Colonel, whether he was speaking to Blaskic with the authority that is revealed here, and whether he was taking these sorts of steps. Now, if he did not at the time, page 2, say things like, I don't mean these precise words, he won't remember that: "Let's have the multiple rocket launcher here. Get it ready for Kacuni." If he knows that was not the sort of thing he could have said, then this witness should have been cross-examined frankly and candidly on that point. Likewise, a few lines further on, if it was his case that he never, could never have said: "Prepare everything. Select the targets for the mortars. Let's burn everything." that should have been put clearly, and it simply wasn't. There are plenty more examples of that. These tapes are, of course, utterly revealing of the true nature of the relationship and of other matters. As a matter of interest, at the foot of page 2, the two boys killed from behind at the checkpoint, is a matter for which there is independent evidence, I think, coming from the Blaskic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had mention of people being killed at Kacuni. I remember it. I think it's been put in cross-examination and, I think, accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour may be right. We have all sorts of other matters of details. For example, on page 2 of the next sector, lines 22 and 23, Mr. Kordic talking to de la Mota, the sort of matter will easily turn up in other evidence, perhaps in the Defence evidence as being capable of proof. At page 4 we have the clear or at least possibly clear evidence that Blaskic is -- that Kordic is referred to in his absence by two others speaking together, at line 25, as a Colonel, and indeed we know that he's actually sought out as a Colonel. I don't want to waste your time too much, but there are plenty of further references of interest. Yes. There we are. Page 11. These are two people, line 29, out of Kordic's presence, referring to him as a Colonel, a matter of real importance and significance, given the timing. Over at page 12 of the same transcript, Kordic and Blaskic talking together. Very well. Line 10: "The people will go out again. "Blaskic: Well, the people should be informed about that. They should go out and block everything, because the potatoes, if they're not used today, we can throw them away. "Listen," says Kordic, "call those people in Kiseljak now and tell them the traffic will be blocked unless the potatoes arrive." The Chamber will have well in mind all the other evidence that there is of linkage between one issue and another, the evidence of the use of civilians to effect objectives. Page 17, line 30, since there are issues raised about the quality of the tape, I dare say on one day the quality may have been different from another. It might explain why the first tape happens to be better than the last ones. There's plenty of evidence. Line -- page -- page 17, line 30. There's plenty of evidence that some at any event, of the time, the line wasn't working very well. "My God, I can't, this phone, /inaudible/ cut off." Page 19, line 26. There's a matter of interest. They seem to have in mind, and perhaps this explained why the conversations dried up, that they were being taped. Well, now there is a whole lot more stuff in these interviews that may turn out to be valuable, may very well turn out to be valuable, but the present position is as clear as can be. This is evidence that the witness brings to your Court. Asked whether there were other matters to be dealt with in detail, Mr. Stein declined the invitation, and let's recall, because it's very important, exactly the history. Tape produced; Defence invited to admit the voice; made clear that if they didn't admit the voice, then the tape would be presented either to other witnesses who could identify the voice or to scientists, if they could do it. The voice had to be admitted, but no discreet challenges to the contents have been made. I think it was suggested by Mr. Stein -- I haven't been able to have access to LiveNote until just now, but I think it was suggested that the witness couldn't say whether there had been the odd inserted word here or deleted word there. There's no point to which he refers where the addition or deletion of the word, even if scientifically possible, could change the sense. They've had the tape long enough to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now in a position to rule on this matter. What we have to decide is whether the evidence relating to this tape should be excluded. The case mounted by the Defence can be summarised in this way: that there has been no evidence from the monitors who heard the tape. We have the evidence of the Intelligence Officer who took charge of it. I think he put it on a tape himself and had custody of it and eventually handed it over, via his superior, to the Office of the Prosecutor. Really, what is said is that there was an opportunity, during the time that the tape was handed over, some three weeks, for somebody to have tampered with it. It was not suggested to the Intelligence Officer that it had been in any way tampered with by him or his two monitors, and it was specifically stated that there was no suggestion that the Office of the Prosecutor had tampered with it. It is also suggested that there are some differences between the tape which the witness handed over and the tape which he kept and was eventually played here, he having brought it with him. Mr. Stein points out that there are two noises and that part of the conversation is missing on one of the tapes. That being the position, we have to ask ourselves, under Rule 95, having ruled as we have done, if the tape should be excluded because it was obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability. I pause to note the words "substantial doubt upon its reliability." I venture to say this: that this witness who was called appeared credible -- I say no more about it at this stage -- in the account which he gave. It is true, as the Defence point out, that he kept no other souvenirs from the war but he kept this one, but he did give an explanation for that. In our judgement, there is nothing to suggest, in the arguments which have been put forward, that this evidence was obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability. That said, we shall exclude the parts which are said not to appear on one of the tapes, and that is conversations 10 and 11. They were described on the English transcript, that is, beginning lines 27 and over the next page on page 18, and ending over the next page, page 19, line 10. That part will be excluded. If there's any further argument in due course about that, we will hear it. Now, the fact that the evidence has been admitted, of course, takes the matter no further than that, and it will be a matter for us to determine, in due course, what weight, if any, we place upon the evidence. We note, I should also add, that there has not been a challenge or a substantial challenge that the voices of Mr. Kordic are those of Mr. Kordic, and therefore, as I say, we will admit this evidence and determine, in the ruling finally, making our judgement, what weight to give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court, only for record purposes, I'm sure Mr. Nice didn't realise he was speaking in error. We received only the first conversation on 9 December 1999. We're then asked to admit or whether we challenged whether it was Mr. Kordic's voice on that, a conversation. On January 18th of this year, we received Mr. Husic's statement and, around that time, the remaining conversations on the tape, and it was only at the date of the hearing that we actually got the wrapper or cassette index itself. I don't think Mr. Nice intentionally miss-spoke, but for the record purposes, if that becomes an issue, I would like to clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the evidence of the tape, of course there should be a public record. But in the event, the first and obviously most important tape was, I think, both played and translated to the public arena. Unless the Court takes a different view, I don't desire particularly to make a public record of the remaining conversations that have been admitted. They are available for the Chamber to consider. If the Defence take a different view, why, of course I would not object to the time being taken in the reading of those interviews. But otherwise I would have thought we could simply leave them with the Chamber for review later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll confer with my colleagues and Mr. Kordic, but our preliminary position is we don't think it's necessary to reinvent the wheel and to replay the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear, in due course, what you say about it. I would have thought it was unnecessary. The most important one has been played, and the others, Mr. Nice has gone through what he thinks is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly the way the emphasis has been put. I suggest there are some different ways to look at that tape, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you should have the opportunity, if there are some matters you would want to draw our attention to, which you would normally do possibly through cross-examination or the like. If there are matters on the tapes which you want to draw our attention to, could you do it fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now turn to the question of transcripts. I'm going to ask Mr. Scott to deal with that on behalf of this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I stand right by here, I can still split, if it's acceptable to the Court, rather than reshuffle things at the desk. Your Honours, may it please the Court, our position on the transcripts is rather straightforward. I'm only going to make a couple of comments about it now. I suspect that there may be things to be said in response to questions the Defence may raise, but suffice it to say for our purposes it's actually, we think, fairly straightforward. We have tendered, Your Honours, to the Defence, over the past several days, first one version and then a second version, and provided to the Court staff yesterday yet another chart, if you will, some 17 pages listing, in alphabetical order, the witnesses which we now propose to present by transcript. I'll pause and say that I think that with perhaps one or two exceptions, but perhaps no exceptions, most of these transcripts come from the Blaskic case. A number of these have been discussed and noted in the past number of months, Your Honours. There has always been, I think, frankly, some contemplation, dating back to at least the consideration of the Tulica dossier, that the Prosecutor would, in fact, ultimately seek to present a number of witnesses by this transcript method. The Court ruled, as I'm sure the Court recalls, in the Tulica decision on July 29th, 1999. At page 11 in its ultimate ruling, in connection with the Tulica binder, the Court stated at paragraph 28: "Accordingly, the Trial Chamber holds that the transcripts of Witnesses NN, OO, and PP," which are also listed on our chart, Your Honour, and I will not say the names of the witnesses here in public session, but the names are on the chart available to the Court. Continuing with the quote: "... are admissible, since the witnesses have been cross-examined in Blaskic, a case in which the Defence have a common interest with the Defence in this case. However, this ruling will not preclude the application by the Defence to cross-examine the witnesses on the ground that there are significant, relevant matters not covered by cross-examination in Blaskic which ought to be raised in this case." And the chart we have prepared, Mr. President, provides exactly for that. It's a rather straightforward chart. If the Court has it in front of it, and I hope it does, there is simply listed the name of the witness, again a summary of what this witness addresses, which Mr. Cerkez' Counsel asked us to add and we did so. There's simply a mark and a place to mark whether the transcript is agreed, and then there is a column for specific objections to the transcript or a statement of the nature and basis of any request for live cross-examinations. We certainly understand, as we think consistent with the Aleksovski Appeal Chamber ruling and this Court's Tulica decision, if I can call it that, that the Defence does have the opportunity to specifically say why they need some additional live cross-examination of the witnesses. While we certainly recognise that opportunity, Your Honour, I take the opportunity -- I guess I take the opportunity to say we can't imagine many instances in which it would be necessary. Many of these are what we've come to call in this case "village witnesses," not entirely but many, and they simply go to the crimes on the ground, so to speak. These identical issues were presented in the Blaskic case. I would say in this case, Your Honour, the relationship or the commonality of interest between the Blaskic Defence and the Kordic Defence is extremely close. They both simply -- apart from evidence that was specific to Kordic or specific to Blaskic, presumably both Defences were intent on proving such things as it wasn't the HVO in the attack, the village was a defended place, certain things, alleged events, didn't in fact happen. Those issues are exactly the same, whether they were presented in the Blaskic case or the Kordic case. Your Honours, that's basically our position. As I say, it's rather straightforward, we think. We have reassessed in the last number of days, in terms of the Court's guidance on scheduling and time limits, this is the most efficient way of presenting this evidence. Frankly, there's a number of these witnesses that, given time, we might very well call live, but we are trying to bring the trial or at least the Prosecution case to a close, and this is the most efficient way of doing so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers is going to speak. There were atrocities in various parts of Central Bosnia. These are facts which in and of themselves have a certain level of objectiveness or objectivity. There is the participation or involvement of the accused, and the relationship between the accused and those events, that's another point. Therefore, we must concentrate on the issue of the events, that is, transcripts that were prepared, because this is the same Tribunal. We must not forget that the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, despite the fact that it has several Trial Chambers, is really one Tribunal, and even if the accused are being heard and tried in different Chambers. Therefore, you must focus on that and make the distinction, if you can. This would be extremely helpful to us, of course, the Trial Chamber, this one or others. To go back to facts already proved in other places, it would be totally absurd, and I'm speaking of the facts themselves. Now, the involvement of the accused, that's another question that has to be judged on a case-by-case basis, but there is relative authority on the things that are being heard. That's the point we've reached, and I would ask you to focus on that because it would be extremely helpful to us. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and to use the vernacular, let me say that I think, from the outset, your comments are pretty much right on the money, and we don't necessarily disagree with any of the points that have been made, other than to say this: In the Blaskic case, I think the defendant in that case had, for whatever reason, made challenges to the existence of some of the events on the ground. In addition, in the Blaskic case the Prosecution articulated a theory of a unitary chain of command in that case, whereas in this case they appear to be articulating a theory that's completely different. So there are some differences in the Defence objectives, if you like, in the Blaskic case as well as in the Prosecution theory. But if I may, let me just step back a little bit and say a few things. First, as I understood it, we were only going to be arguing about eight transcript witnesses today, and I would point out that those aren't village witnesses at all. And those eight witnesses are included in the 49 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have, for example, a Member of Parliament, the British parliament, Mr. Ashdown. We have a number of yet more, if I may say, European Community Monitoring Mission monitors and many soldiers in the British Army. Of course, we have heard a lot of that evidence. But I'm prepared to address the eight transcript witnesses specifically. I also would like to address, perhaps this is the best way to start out, the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber decision, because I think there's been some lack of attention paid to precisely what that decision says, and I'd like to go through it in some detail with the Trial Chamber. I'd like to present that argument, and then Mr. Stein will address the more general issue of these transcript witnesses, and I'm sure he will point out that approximately 50 per cent of the case that the Prosecution, therefore, seeks to make out against Mr. Kordic will come in by way of transcript evidence from witnesses that he's never had the opportunity to confront or cross-examine. I think that that's a potentially significant problem, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? Are there any transcripts which you would be prepared to admit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we start with that and then we know what's left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might, Mr. President -- perhaps it makes sense just to articulate our view of the Aleksovski decision and then proceed to the transcripts that we don't have a problem with. Fundamentally, I think, and of course, Mr. President, since you were the author, I'm -- you'll correct me if I'm wrong, I'm sure, but the decision in Aleksovski was fundamentally a hearsay decision, and really, a decision was made on two separate points. One is called the first decision, and that's paragraphs 14 through 21 of the decision, and then under an equality-of-arms rationale, the Court made a decision on the so-called second decision, paragraphs 22 to 28. I think it's important to underscore the procedural context in which the applications for the admission of transcript evidence came before the Trial Chamber in Aleksovski. Notable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We should have the Aleksovski decision in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I've a copy of it here if you need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I see. We have it on the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Procedural context was as follows: The Prosecution's case-in-chief lasted three months, from January to March of 1998. The Defence then presented its case. The Prosecution presented rebuttal evidence on one day, September the 22nd, 1998, and an application to receive the evidence of Admiral Dvor Domazet, who testified in Blaskic on September the 10th, was made on December the 29th, which was after the Prosecution had presented its rebuttal case. The Prosecution obviously objected. The Trial Chamber's decision in that case was entered on 22nd of October, which was two days after the Defence rejoinder case had closed. The Trial Chamber's decision had, and we would submit -- and you can find this at page 4, paragraph 7(A) and 7(B) of the decision -- two significant underpinnings. The first was -- and I think this is extremely important from the perspective of this proposal to have the Aleksovski decision serve as a wholesale passport for huge quantities of evidence from other cases into this case. In fact, I think the 49 or 46 witnesses referred to on the document that we received yesterday spend no less than 13,000 pages of testimony, and I would point out to the Trial Chamber that that's exclusive of General Blaskic's testimony which in itself spans some 6,000 pages. But the point that the Aleksovski Court made was -- the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber, was that the evidence first has to be of indisputable probative value, and that was on the international armed conflict issue in that case. But equally significant was the situation was exceptional, and it was exceptional because Admiral Domazet was not available to testify. The trial had reached its final phase, Mr. Aleksovski had been in custody for one a half years, but more importantly, it was the Prosecution, Your Honours, the Prosecution that had already had the opportunity to examine and cross-examine Admiral Domazet and had done so at great length in that case. So the very party against whom, if you like, the testimony of Admiral Domazet was being introduced, the very party against whom that testimony was being introduced had had the opportunity itself to cross-examine that witness at length. And of course, as was pointed out in the dissent in Aleksovski, Admiral Domazet was actually an expert witness. Now, there were two separate rulings, and I think that those rulings are significant because they're -- they proceed on two different bases. The first argument relating to Mr. Aleksovski's argument that Admiral Domazet's testimony should be introduced had a hearsay underpinning. Hearsay had to be reliable, and the Court obviously cited the Tadic factors, but this was an exception to the general principle that witnesses should be heard directly under principle of orality enshrined in Rule 90(A), but that was found to be subject to the discretion of the Trial Chamber. And the Aleksovski decision found that the Trial Chamber had not abused its discretion. The Trial Chamber had the discretion under Rule 90(A) to admit relevant and reliable information in those exceptional circumstances. One transcript we were talking about in the Aleksovski case. And under the consideration that the witness was not immediately available himself to testify in person, which apparently was what the defendant in Aleksovski had preferred, in the absence of the declarant, to use a hearsay term, being available, the Court said that was an essential circumstance and in existential circumstance, given the stage of the case and the fact that the Prosecution had already cross-examined him, that was an appropriate application, and the Appeals Chamber said that since that was a matter of discretion, it could not say that the discretion had been abused in that one instance. Furthermore, the Court proceeded to observe in Aleksovski that no attempt had been made by the Prosecution to show any particular line of cross-examination that would have been both relevant and significant that was not already pursued in the Blaskic case. Now, the second decision was reached on a point that was completely different from the first decision, and it was an equality-of-arms decision. The Prosecution had argued that if the Defence should be permitted to introduce Admiral Domazet's testimony under the unusual and exceptional circumstances in which that application had been made, then under an equality of means or equality of rights, I'll avoid the term "equality of arms," but under an equality of means analysis, then the testimony of the confidential witnesses that the Prosecution sought to be adduced, that that should be permissible too, but that was only because, in the first instance, in the exceptional circumstances evidence of indisputable probative value had been permitted to be introduced by way of transcript at the application of the Defence. So you have a hearsay analysis, exceptional circumstances which are the hallmarks of the first decision, and then the second decision is an equality-of-arms decision. Now, there was a vociferous dissent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The dissent in the case made the point that the right to cross-examination is an essential component of most systems of law and, arguably, the failure to provide for such a right is inconsistent with the international covenant on civilian and political rights. But I think what we were -- what was under consideration in Aleksovski was, I believe, three transcripts. One that the defendant sought to have introduced and then, two, under an equality-of-arms theory that the Prosecution sought to have adduced. That brings me -- and I think I've accurately represented what the holding of the Court was, what the procedural context was, and what the essential point made by the dissent was. And that brings us, if we may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can remind me where the point is made about exceptional circumstances in the first decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Paragraph 7(B), page 4, where the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the Trial Chamber decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Correct. The situation was exceptional, Admiral Domazet was not immediately available due to the nature of his duties, the trial had reached its final phase, and the accused Aleksovski had been in custody since April the 29th, 1997. As you point out, Mr. President, that was what the Trial Chamber ruled in deciding that the testimony of Admiral Domazet in the Blaskic case should be imported into the Aleksovski case. The point that I was making was that the Appeals Chamber said that that decision was not an abuse of discretion. So the first decision, if you like, the hearsay decision, was really reviewed or really -- the basis of it was an abuse of discretion, and the analysis was had -- under the circumstances presented, had the Trial Chamber in Aleksovski abused its discretion? It was no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What part of the judgement supports that, that the Appeals Chamber's ruling was in support of what you have just referred to, the exceptional nature and there was no abuse of discretion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Paragraph 21, Judge Robinson -- or Your Honour. I'm sorry. It says: "It follows that no criticism had been made of the Trial Chamber in the exercise of its discretion, and the appeal against the first decision fails." That's on page 10 of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And pages 9, at the very bottom, paragraph 19. "These circumstances, the Trial Chamber was entitled to take account, at the stage of the trial, the length of time that the accused had been in custody and its finding that the witness was not immediately available in exercising its discretion to admit the evidence."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's precisely -- that's precisely right. According --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're saying that it's only in exceptional circumstances that transcript evidence may be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, if I may be a bit more pragmatic than that, Mr. President. We are fully aware that these trials take a long time. We don't want to drag them out for any longer than they have to. Looking at the Aleksovski decision, we do take the view of it that it is an exception rather than the rule, but that exception -- our interpretation of the exception, if you like, has to be tempered by a certain pragmatism, and I think that it is appropriate to take a look at each individual witness to see whether they offer testimony that is particular to the accused. If the evidence, of course, is particular to the accused then there is an elevated need for cross-examination of that witness. If, on the other hand, the witness testifies basically to, as His Honour Judge Bennouna said, objective events about which there can be little contest and which have been extensively cross-examined by someone who had an interest that's allied with the defendant in this particular case, then a very good argument could be made that there's very little reason for the transcript of such a witness not to be introduced in this case. And it's with that observation that I turn, if I may, to each of the individual witnesses. I take it from your comments to me yesterday, Mr. President, that you have in mind the November the 10th, 1999 document that was delivered to us. Let me just address these issues -- each witness, witness by witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witnesses are repeated in the overall document. We have 46 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We could find them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to the first witness. I believe that this witness testified in closed session in both the Blaskic and the Kupreskic cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got it. We better get the number on the new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The new number is on page 4, witness number 10, Your Honour. Now, let me just start out by -- a few comments are appropriate in connection with this witness, Your Honour. This witness supposedly talks about killings in Busovaca that were ordered by Kordic. I do -- I believe that there is not any. In the Kupreskic case, the witness testified for 117 pages and the same is true; no contentions to support that -- or no testimony to support the contention made on page 4. But let me say with respect to this witness, Your Honour, this is an important individual. He was a Muslim who was -- I mean, he had a remarkable career. He was in the HOS. He was in the Patriotic League for a time. He, I believe, spent time in the TO. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Eight is number 46 on the most recent document.

utterances.text: And apparently six diplomatic dispatches were provided to Defence Counsel, and there was fairly significant questioning based upon those diplomatic dispatches. utterances.text: Now, as far as the other witnesses are concerned, how long do you think it's going to take you? I mean, it may be sensible to look at another batch next week, because we shall not be here the week after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour Judge Bennouna, that is something we are doing. But for some things, we do need some input from our client. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wonder if you can assist in this. I mean the suggestion that the Chamber, let alone the Defence, has 13,000 pages of transcript, whether that's right or not, to assimilate at this stage is a burden of a very considerable kind, and I really wonder whether it's necessary to have this number of witnesses. Now, of course there are one or two details which he adds, but we really do have a very clear picture, I think, of what happened in Ahmici. The question must be whether it's going to assist us to have even more detail. It may well be that what the witness said isn't in dispute. But you might like, during the week, to conduct a further consideration with a view to concentrating on those witnesses which are really important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, we will do that. At this point, though, the number of pages reflects frequently the fact that witnesses have given evidence on more than one occasion and probably, in procedural terms, less efficiently than perhaps witnesses who have been giving evidence here. Secondly, although the whole transcript is identified, Your Honour is quite right, it might only be for one short point that the transcript is required. Thus far, the Defence have, I think, taken the position publicly that a part in all in, and of course if we were to put in the transcript or seek to put in the transcript of the witness Hughes for one point, a piece of artillery or something of that sort, and there was a part that they wanted, of course it would go before you in those circumstances, this without prejudice to the Blaskic argument. But that doesn't require the Judges or any of those working with the Judges to read all of the transcript, because in due course there would be direction as to which parts would be required to be read. Apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you might like to look at it from this point too. It is often said in these long cases that -- and juries, as you know, are always warned not to lose sight of the wood for the trees. Now, even professional Judges would have to warn themselves in the same way, and the question is does it assist us to have this huge amount of detail as opposed to concentrating on what are emerging as the central issues in the case. With that in mind, I would suggest that a great number of these witnesses could be culled from the list. As far as I can see, most of the indictment, if not all of it -- I haven't checked -- has been covered. Of course, if there was some particular matter, then you would be entitled to call evidence. But where it's repetitive of evidence that we've already heard and there has been little or no challenge, or challenge purely of a formal nature, it may be that the Prosecution could take a view about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll be responsive to Your Honour's suggestion. I well understand it, and it may be that our response will take two forms; one to delete names, the other to say, "But this witness would only be required by the Prosecution on this narrow topic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May I point out one other problem, and of course you'll immediately see I'm doing it to my advantage, and that is that should a large amount of transcript be grafted onto this proceeding, it would be our position it would be necessary for the Court to review that in order to rule on our motion for judgement of acquittal. The smile on my face is because I would then say, "Then perhaps you want to give us a little more time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I mean clearly by the end of the case, we would have had to have reviewed all the evidence. We couldn't do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Unless we, by agreement, extend the time for that motion and thereby extend the time to start our case, and that's why I thought I would announced I was trying to be a tad, shall we say, humorous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for being in tandem with Mr. Nice on this, but if I could make a couple of comments, only because I think it would move us forward. I had not yet had a chance to respond to a couple of points made by the Defence. Let me tell the Court, these summaries are, if you will, general-purpose summaries. We have not had time to generate yet another version of summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If there are things in the summary, for instance, some of the things pointed out like the last sentence of the summary in his particular case, and if that's not in the transcript, then there's really no reason for the Defence to be concerned about it. I say that because it very well might be possible to either clarify or omit certain passages if we simply say, "All right, we delete lines 23 to 28 of page 16 that you don't like because we don't need it." So we need, I request, Your Honour, some specificity from the Defence, because we may be able to obviate many of the problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the Defence hear that? If there are -- particularly for passages which are objected to, again if that could be identified, the rest of the evidence could go in but with a deletion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and we will take that to heart. I remind everyone, however, we have some other things going on next week like exhibits, dossiers, et cetera. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for a break. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We turn to the village dossiers, and let me remind you of what we held in Tulica, which, summarising the matter, was that we were against the witness statements. utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honour, we, by agreement with Mr. Scott, have agreed to discuss Zenica, Busovaca, and Zepce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the three that were mentioned yesterday which we have in mind. Starting with -- Mr. Lopez-Terres, on Zenica, on the list of witnesses, John Hamill is mentioned. Is he going to be called?

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the statements, the transcripts of the statements, there are several witnesses who appear on the list about whom we were speaking before the break. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. On the list referring to the Zenica shelling, it is Witness number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Stein or Mr. Sayers, whoever is dealing with this -- Mr. Sayers, the position is that these are mostly exhibits, except for various transcripts. utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. President, that the Tulica decision absolutely deals with this. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. No doubt that could be provided, Mr. Lopez-Terres, and we'll hear from the Defence when it has been. Shall we move to the next binder. If I could hand this one back. utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, documents that were not yet produced are death certificates.

utterances.text: Just tracking down on the categories indicated on the index, Mr. President, item number 2, we remain opposed to the admission of witness statements and we have nothing to add to our previous positions on that.

utterances.text: I mean that's not sought, to admit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the transcript references, nothing to add. With respect to the maps, I think they're already in evidence. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I recollect, there's been evidence about the deaths of some of these people. An early witness did deal with that, aspects of it, funerals and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, of course, some of them are unexplained, yes. These documents can only be introduced for what they show, presumably death and a date. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we also agree that a standard has already been set by your ruling on Tulica, and we are quite happy with that. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The only thing I wanted to say was that in the case of Tulica, you asked both Defences to pronounce themselves, and we did that. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm now returning to the third village binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before we do, while Mr. Lopez-Terres and Mr. Scott change places, I think, there's a general point that I want to raise. It arises from the precise wording of your decision in Tulica in relation to statements. It's at page 9, and what the Chamber said was that it's of the view that whilst it could admit the witness statements under Rule 89(C), this is not an appropriate case for the exercise of its discretion under that provision, as it would amount to the wholesale -- for these purposes, I emphasise that word; it's not otherwise emphasised -- the wholesale admission of hearsay untested by cross-examination, mainly the attack on Tulica, will be of no probative value. The Trial Chamber therefore declines to admit the witness statements into evidence; however, draws attention to Rule 94 ter of the Rules. Since then, and indeed before then, we've been tussling with and making the slowest possible progress with 94 ter, but the ruling plainly allows of the possibility of adduction for evidence of witness statements, and we are now in the position, of course, where the honing down of the case means that there are only one or two witnesses, or whatever it is, per village on whom we rely now to prove the facts of the crimes on the ground. I have to say that if and when those witnesses come to give evidence, they'll be taken very shortly, and it may indeed be the time has come for literally, "I adopt my statement," particularly if the witnesses say absolutely nothing about either defendant, and it will be regrettable in the extreme if their evidence, given in that way or in any other way, is subject to no cross-examination. There are two ways in which this material could be presented to the Chamber more efficiently and more swiftly where there is really no contest. One is the Defence could approach us and say, "Yes, well, we don't need that witness. That witness can, in fact, be read." I've made so many requests in the past that I'm not going to embarrass myself by a further solicitation that is likely for me to get nowhere, but they could do that. The alternative is, quite in line with your ruling, in respect of these individual witnesses who simply prove the on-the-ground attacks, the Chamber could possibly invite the Defence to indicate what, if any, significant cross-examination there is to be, because in the absence of any, it might be that the attendance of witnesses, simply to acknowledge their statements or to give the shortest possible evidence, could be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are there any witnesses whom you want to deal with by way of a statement? And I'm not going to encourage you to do that, because our ruling, although it did allow the possibility of it, was largely against such a course. Then I think you must indicate who the witnesses are, and we'll consider them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott may do that in Zepce, and I'll have another word with Mr. Lopez-Terres while he's doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, there seems to be -- there's a summary which I didn't mention, but unless you're seeking to get it in in Tulica, we rule the summary out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's merely there, as I understand it, for your -- to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But that's not admissible. Then we have a map, we have a census, a video. We then have three statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Those are the statements of the two witnesses in that particular regard that we would propose to call as live -- short of what Mr. Nice has just stated, that we would propose to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Then as far as the documents are concerned, there's a list of deceased persons, a list of detainees, another map and various plans, further lists of detainees, and death certificates. Yes. You seek to admit all those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Sayers -- Mr. Stein, the witnesses are apparently to be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with that first, sir. That was the subject of a Prosecution appeal to the Appeals Chamber, which was turned down. Those issues are adequately set out at day 27 of the June 3rd, 1999 record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, let me stop you for a minute. You're saying that we ruled this evidence inadmissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fahrudin Poturovic. I must say it escaped my memory, that -- specifically that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. There were at least three or four that were subject to the exclusionary rule that Your Honour applied. It was all due to late disclosure. They're specifically set out at the Prosecution's appeal. Yes. There were four, Ifran Ajanovic, the witness in question, Mr. Babic, and Mr. Huremovic. All four were excluded on the basis of that order. The Prosecution appealed. I think there's no sense to beat a dead horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What about the other matters? Is there any dispute about any of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I would note, sir, that as to the census, there's the two pages. I don't want to stand on much ceremony. The first makes no sense. The second is indeed a summary as set out in the three footnotes. It's a Prosecutor's summary. It's really not the census. For what it's worth, it's worthless. It may or may not be in evidence. We have no objection to the video. As to the documents, we have no objection to 5.2, the lists of the deceased. That's already in evidence. The rest of the documents, there's no source attached; that is to say, there is a list of names of persons imprisoned in the elementary school at 5.3. There's no source given. At 5.4 is a hand-drawn map by the witness Maglic. Same thing with 5.5, hand-drawn cells. I really don't think they'll be helpful. As well as 5.6, hand-drawn maps of the Silos. Besides being no proper foundation, I don't think they're going to help the Court. More germane, 5.7 and 5.8 are names of Muslims held in the five hangars and lists of Muslims captured. There's no source given to how those lists came into being, whose lists they are, or the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a matter of weight, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course, sir. You just don't even know who to put it to, who to attach it to. And then the death certificates, of course, we have no problem with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit the documents, but, Mr. Scott, if it's right that Mr. Poturovic is already the subject of a ruling, then there's no need -- there's no possibility of your calling him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I specifically wanted to raise that and Mr. Ajanovic with the Court and had it on my notes to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't wish there to be any impression that we were trying to slide that by, but in the order of things we went to the documents. Your Honour, the three witnesses that we would present, select to call live, and Mr. Stein is absolutely correct on this point, include Mr. Poturovic, and I come to also include this morning and ask the Court's leave to call Mr. Irfan Ajanovic. Before we turn back to those, the third is Taib Sehic, about whom there apparently is no dispute. Let me do this very briefly, Your Honour. We have said, as the Court knows, virtually from day one, perhaps even before the trial started, that there were some -- there began to be some notions of something like two witnesses per village, never written in stone, but something along those lines. It's absolutely correct that Mr. Poturovic and Mr. Ajanovic were among those two of the four that were excluded, I think in June, on the 3rd of June last year. We absolutely say that openly, acknowledge that. We asked the Court to review that, and your argument is this: There is no disclosure issue concerning these two. These statements have now been turned over, were turned over in May. There simply can be no surprise to the Defence. As we try to conclude this case, Your Honour, as we're trying very hard to do by the 10th of March, these are, if we have to pick and choose the witnesses to present on the two-per-village rule, these would be among those that we would choose to provide, Your Honour, recognising that we're now at a point in the trial, the Prosecution has to pick those witnesses and that evidence to present in the final stages before the 10th, and I would ask the Court, respectfully, that there being no bona fide disclosure issue, having been disclosed some eight months ago, but as we conclude the case, the Prosecution should be able to call what it views to be the best witnesses on this particular city or village, Zepce. We think there's simply no prejudice to the Defence at this point, and we would ask the Court, acknowledging the Court's prior ruling, that we ask the Court to allow us to call -- to make our selection of those village witnesses to include those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've had at least one witness on Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't think it's in closed, is it? It's a protected witness, Your Honour, but the Court is correct. If it's sufficiently important we go to private session, but there is -- there's only been, Your Honour, to date one witness on Zepce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've ruled in the case of one witness, and Judge Robinson points out that it's a matter which is res judicata, I suppose there may be discretion to reopen old decisions, but if there is, we're not going to take it. Now, that's the binders. There are a number outstanding. Those are the ones for today. Kiseljak, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. There is a discreet issue in relation to Tulica itself, but Mr. Lopez-Terres suggests that it can probably be dealt with when Kiseljak is reviewed. Parties have staked out positions in correspondence, and I don't think there's much point in taking time with it today. We can deal with it with Kiseljak, which I think we'll be dealing with on the 14th when we're going to deal with all outstanding village binders, I hope. We will, I trust, between now and then, notify the Defence of any witnesses who we say should be read, and we'll try and notify the Chamber between now and then similarly of what witnesses we say should be read or could be read in order to save time. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before 12 o’clock, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now that the tape and its transcript have been admitted, the outstanding small issue on Hadzihasanovic seems to be capable of being disposed of. We don't require him. The Court has already indicated it doesn't either. He, therefore, won't come. The same topic. The Chamber will recall that at the application to exclude, the evidence was read of the telephone official who diverted the call. That's part of the transcript. I don't know that I particularly need that witness for my case in any event, although he has presently arranged to come in the week after next. All he's going to say is what's contained in the statement. I don't know whether the Defence are going to make any point about the admissibility of what he's already said in the statement, in the trial, or whether they're going to admit it or what. I better not give the name in case he seeks protection, but the Chamber will probably be able to find it, and if not, I probably will be able to provide a copy. Maybe I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is he on the list which we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, he -- no. I'm not sure that he is on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No matter. No matter. Is there any reason why the Defence want him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, not at all. We agreed to have him read out as part of the preliminary matter. It's, in our view, incorporated by reference in the record, as I said. I'm surprised there's an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I think that is, and I might be wrong, the first statement that's -- read statement that's gone in. I'm grateful. The next issue is documents generally and the document production. As we know, the Defence are going to notify us as soon as may be of any documents the provenance of which is doubted. The date was to be today but has understandably has been extended. We know so far of only a few documents whose provenance is challenged, and we are making arrangements to call witnesses to prove those. It will obviously be more satisfactory if we can deal with that issue on a -- as a single topic and call the witness or witnesses necessary at an identified date. May we have, perhaps, a revised timetable of when we'll be notified of what documents are challenged as to their provenance? It will assist us. And before I sit down, because the following topic, short as it is, may also require an order, I don't know, videos, for example, videos of meetings involving Mr. Kordic, that sort of thing, there has, I think, been an issue as to whether they can be produced other than by a participating witness. That, with respect, must, I think, be wrong. A witness can simply produce a video. "I produce this video," says the witness. "It was handed to me by 'X' or 'Y.'" But in fact, I think, it's clearly the case in this Tribunal that -- not necessarily this Chamber but in this Tribunal that such material is typically accepted without any cumbersome procedure as to receipt and provenance where there's no purpose to be served in those issues taking the time of the Court. The Chamber will remember, I think, a social anthropologist whose tape was simply played, and it may have been introduced by an expert nominally, but the tape was simply played. We've got a number of tapes, videotapes of one type and another, and in principle, providing they meet the test of relevance, it's our view that they should simply be admitted without the cumbersome procedure of producing someone to produce them, whether a participating witness or otherwise. It will be rather like the aerial video. Of course Colonel Capelle was able to say something about it, but if he hadn't been around, probably it would have been acceptable and admissible because it spoke for itself. Those are the only matters that are outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. We'll have our work done by Monday, the 14th. All of it, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: However, let me be clear on two things. As to the documents, it is my view that we will have a template or working with the Prosecution to get our computer, their computer, and literally give you yes, no, and why. The videos are in total disarray. We don't know what we have, what they've given, what they want. We -- there's been a series of communications between. I'm less sanguine on that. I rise, however, to make one final observation, if I may. We will endeavour to work 16 hours a day next week to get everything behind us, the village dossiers; the documents; what we can of the videos; the transcripts, 12,000 pages, but that's the end. Any other submissions thereafter, it is our view they're for pure tactical gain and advantage. We are now going to focus on our case, I hope, so that we can put on a neat, tidy, compact case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Two small additions, Your Honour, if I may. First, videotapes, confusion -- there is really confusion. And second, we are expecting to have argument on that. There is an open proposal of the Prosecution to tender all the video material simply in the case without any argument on that and criticism. For example, I do have -- I have them in my bag today. I do have two examples of the videos on which I will try to show why we cannot allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll allow time for that, but again, if you could indicate what's admitted and what isn't to the Prosecution so that they know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That goes without saying. And if I just may, just for a second, which our colleague Prosecutor raised on the beginning of today's argument concerning the affidavits or whatever they will be in their form which are planned to be taken in Bosnia. I fear that that is a certain problem. We did investigate the current law there, and from that what was said this morning -- I'm not sure I understood everything correctly -- there is either a new law enacted or there is some mechanism invented which is trying to avoid the law. So I would suggest that the Trial Chamber orders the Prosecutor to inform us which is the legal base in Bosnia to go on that agreement with the Federation, that they will appoint a Judge, and by the way, yesterday it was said Muslim Judge, so there is obviously some discussion. So what is the legal base for that agreement so we can investigate that and check and, second, to give us a copy of the request which will be sent by the Prosecution to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that we may follow up the legal aspect of that, because we see -- and we did check that -- that the only legal possibility in Bosnian is so-called international assistance in criminal matters, which means the Judge/investigator is summoning the witness, the witness is giving a statement in front of the Judge. It is not just authentication of identity or his signature. He is giving a statement, and the Defence is entitled to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see what they produce. When they produce it, we will rule upon it. Now, unless there are any other matters. Very well. Half past 9 Monday next week.
